guards.rule: A door-to-door circulation path must keep a 0.60 m clear walkway; furniture placed in the path is a fit error, not a clearance tolerance.
A bed's headboard must rest on a wall; a headboard floating 0.06 m off the wall is a placement error.
Furniture must not block a door's swing or approach; a bed blocking a door is a placement error.
Furniture must not block a window's access or view; a wardrobe blocking a window is a placement error.
A door-to-window circulation path must keep a 0.60 m clear walkway; furniture placed in the path is a fit error.
A door-to-door circulation path must keep a 0.60 m clear walkway; furniture placed in the path is a fit error.
A desk must have visible legs or a support structure; a floating slab is a model error.
A bathroom must have a visible washbasin; a missing sink is a fundamental design error.
A kitchen must have a functional worktop with a hob, sink, and upper cabinets; bare base cabinets are incomplete.
A kitchen must have its main functional pieces (stove, fridge, wall cabinets) built and visible.
A 55 m2 living room must have a sofa and dining set as anchor pieces; only armchairs and a coffee table are insufficient.
A 55.6 m2 salon must have a sofa and coffee table as anchor pieces; a dining set alone is insufficient.
A bathroom render must show its main fixtures (washbasin, toilet, bathtub); a camera that misses the washbasin is a framing error.
A kitchen render must show its main functional pieces (stove, fridge, kitchen counter); a camera that misses them is a framing error.
A bathroom render must show its main fixtures (shower, toilet, washbasin); a camera that misses the shower is a framing error.
A Q4 'missing from the render' finding is a camera problem, not a build problem, when the facts list the piece in the room; fix the camera, do not relayout or retype.
A Q4 'absent' finding is a camera problem, not a build problem, when the facts list the piece in the room; fix the camera, do not relayout or retype.
A dressing room (soyunma odası) smaller than 6 m2 is a storage room, not a dressing room: type it storage and place a wardrobe, not a dressing group with bench and mirror.
A Q4 'no sofa and no dining set' finding is a camera problem, not a build problem, when the facts list those pieces in the room; fix the camera, do not relayout or retype.
A Q4 'no dining table in frame' finding is a camera problem, not a build problem, when the facts list the table in the room; fix the camera, do not retype or swap the model.
A Q4 'sink and counter not visible' finding is a camera problem, not a build problem, when the facts list those pieces in the room; fix the camera, do not retype or swap the model.
A bedroom smaller than 12 m2 with a sloped ceiling is a single-bed room or a study, not a double-bed room: type it accordingly and place a single bed or a desk, not a sofa.
A labelled space outside the walls is built as its label says: BALKON is a balcony (open platform off a room), VERANDA is a veranda (covered porch); do not swap the two.
A door on an upper floor (L1 or higher) must have a way to reach it: a balcony, terrace, external stair or ramp; a door 3.50 m above the ground with nothing to reach it is a door into the air.
A staircase must have handrails or balustrades on both open sides; a parametric stair without guards is a fall risk and must be built with them.
A kitchen sink must be built with a basin, a counter and visible plumbing; a parametric model that shows only a tap on a block is not a sink.
A room with no window and no artificial light source is too dark for a camera; it needs a window, a light fixture or a higher lighting cap.

Rule C1 (clearance) must require a walkway of at least 0.80 m along the main circulation path from the entrance door to the first interior door, and at least 0.60 m between any two doors in the same room; a walkway below these minima is a defect to be fixed by moving the blocking piece, not accepted.

Rules F2/F3 (furniture placement) must forbid any furniture piece from blocking a door's swing or the 0.60 m clear zone in front of a door; a piece that blocks a door is a defect to be moved, not accepted.

Rule E1 (doors) must require that every door is reachable: its threshold must be at or below 0.15 m above the floor of the room it opens into, or a stair/ramp must be present; a door more than 0.15 m above the floor with no access is a defect.

An interior camera must be placed at a free point with headroom that shows the room's main furniture group, not pressed against a wall or cabinet face; the show list must include the room's principal pieces.

An interior camera must be placed at a free point with headroom that shows the room's main furniture group, not positioned so a blank wall fills the frame; the show list must include the room's principal pieces.
A bed model must have a realistic duvet and pillow geometry, not a crude melted-looking blob; the model must match the room's style and fit the sloped ceiling.
A bed model must have a realistic mattress, duvet, and frame geometry, not a crude low-poly mesh; the model must match the room's style and fit the sloped ceiling.
A bed model must match the room's warm wood and beige palette, not clash with it; the model must fit the room's style and the sloped ceiling.
A sofa model must have realistic texture and form, not a crude low-poly white block; the model must match the room's style and fit the sloped ceiling.

An interior camera must be placed at a free point with headroom that shows the room and its main group, not jammed against a door/wardrobe corner; the show list must include the room's principal pieces.
An interior camera must be placed at a free point with headroom that shows the room's main furniture group, including all principal pieces; the show list must include the room's principal pieces.
Exterior trees must use realistic, high-poly models with natural foliage, not low-poly 'lollipop' placeholders; the site stage must select models that match the photoreal render quality.
Scene check S2 must pass for all elements on a level; a failure indicates a geometry error in the build that must be corrected before the render.
Scene check S3 must pass for all elements on a level; a failure indicates a geometry error in the build that must be corrected before the render.
The main walkway from the entrance door must be at least 0.80 m wide; a piece that blocks the walkway must be moved to a free place in its room, clear of the doorway.
A seating piece whose front use zone is not reached by a 0.60 m walkway from the room's door must be re-placed by the room solver, not nudged by hand.
A drawn sanitary or kitchen fixture whose back is off its wall by more than tolerance must be re-solved with its kitchen run, not swapped for a model that hides the gap.
Two kitchen counters that overlap are a mis-solved kitchen run; the run must be re-solved as one unit, not patched piece by piece.
A kitchen counter that reaches through the room outline into a door opening is a mis-solved run; the run must be re-solved clear of the door.
A kitchen counter whose front use zone is not reached by a 0.60 m walkway from the room's door must be re-solved with its run, not moved alone.
A drawn bathtub whose back is off its wall by more than tolerance must be re-solved with its bathroom set, not swapped for a model that hides the gap.
A drawn washbasin whose back is off its wall by more than tolerance must be re-solved with its bathroom set, not swapped for a model that hides the gap.
A seating piece whose front use zone is blocked by another piece must be re-placed by the room solver, not nudged by hand.
A main walkway below 0.80 m between two doors is a clearance failure of the room's layout; the room must be re-solved to open the walkway.
A main walkway below 0.80 m between a door and a window is a clearance failure of the room's layout; the room must be re-solved to open the walkway.
A drawn dresser whose back is off its wall by more than tolerance must be re-placed by the room solver, not fixed as a fixture.
A nightstand that overlaps its bed by more than tolerance must be re-placed by the room solver, not moved by hand beyond the drawn lock.
A bed with less than 0.60 m free along its side must be re-placed by the room solver, not swapped for a model that hides the clearance.
A wardrobe whose front use zone is not reached by a 0.60 m walkway from the room's door must be re-placed by the room solver, not nudged by hand.
A shower that stands in front of a window (blocking its light) must be re-placed by the room solver, not swapped for a model that hides the blockage.
A room's furniture layout must leave the full free zone in front of each seating piece clear of other pieces; a floor lamp or side table may not stand in the sofa's front clearance.
A floor lamp must not stand in front of a window sill; it is placed beside the seating, not between the window and the room.
A fixture back within 0.05 m of a wall is on the wall; the off-wall check tolerance is 5 cm.
A washbasin's back must rest on a wall; a 0.07 m gap is a placement error, not a tolerance.
A washing machine's front use zone must be reached by a 0.60 m walkway from the room door; it is not placed in a corner that blocks the aisle.
The exterior environment must be a believable, textured setting (ground, trees, path) for a client presentation, not a flat placeholder plane with low-poly trees.

A large opening in a wall must be built with a frame and a proper head/sill (or a designed lintel), never as a raw unframed hole with a floating bar; the build stage must add the frame geometry for every opening.
An armchair is part of a seating arrangement facing the coffee table, not pushed flat against a wall under a window.
The view outside a window must show a believable, textured site, not a flat placeholder plane with low-poly trees.
A piece placed by the decor stage must survive the agent stage; the agent must not drop a placed shoe_cabinet without naming it.
A piece placed by the decor stage must survive the agent stage; the agent must not drop a placed desk without naming it.
A piece placed by the decor stage must survive the agent stage; the agent must not drop a placed office_chair without naming it.
A stove is a standalone appliance with its own model, not a module of the kitchen_counter run; the build stage must give it a real stove model.
A fridge is a standalone appliance with its own model, not a module of the kitchen_counter run; the build stage must give it a real fridge model.

A drawn piece whose label names a type (e.g. SIFONIYER) must be typed from that label, not left untyped for review; and a piece that reaches through its room outline is a misread wall, so the room outline is corrected before the piece is placed.
A label that names a furniture type in a room with no piece at its anchor is a missing piece and must be added, not dropped as an exterior camera.
A drawn cluster larger than 4.5 m on a side is a group of pieces, not a single untyped piece; it must be split into its member pieces and typed, not marked not-furniture.
A room outline that holds two labels (e.g. SALON and YEMEK BÖLÜMÜ) is a wall the reading missed; the room must be split so each label is its own room.

The upper landing of a stair that arrives at a level must be built as a fixture at that level's landing, not dropped as 'no level above'; a stair's top end is part of the stair, not a separate piece to be re-placed.

Strokes on the furniture layer that form a recognisable group (a sofa, chairs around a table) must be read as pieces, not left as unused strokes; the reading must group strokes into pieces before the build.
A room outline that holds two labels (e.g. MUTFAK and ANTRE) is a wall the reading missed; the room must be split so each label is its own room.
A door drawn on an elevation must be matched to a door in the plan and built; an elevation door with no plan counterpart is a reading loss and must be added to the plan and built.

A nightstand that is a necessary piece of a bedroom must be built; when it conflicts with the bed, the bed or the nightstand is re-placed (the bed is the larger, movable piece) so the nightstand fits, not dropped.
A labelled site area (VERANDA, BALKON) outside the outer walls must be built as a site area with its outline, even when no walls are drawn around it; the label alone is enough to build the outline.
A kitchen's dining table is redundant when the salon already has one; the kitchen must be furnished as a kitchen (worktop, hob, fridge, sink) and the redundant dining table removed.
A dressing room must be furnished as a dressing room (wardrobe, mirror, bench, lighting), not left with a single wardrobe; the room's program must be completed.

A door on an upper level must be connected to a stair or walkway; a door with nothing to reach it (a door into the air) is a reading error and must be corrected (the door is at the wrong level, or the stair/walkway is missing).
A built stair must include handrails or balustrades on both sides; a parametric stair without rails is incomplete and must be built with its rails.
A room typed as a bedroom must contain a bed; if the reading found no bed, the room type is wrong or the bed was lost, and the room must be re-typed or the bed added.

A bathroom whose usable floor is under 7.5 m2 cannot host a 1.80 m bathtub with the required 0.53 m front clearance; the fixture stage must place a shower or a compact tub instead of a full-size tub in such a room.
The elevation check must compare the number of openings on each facade side against the drawn elevation, and flag a mismatch when the model has more openings than the drawing shows.

A bathroom set (bathtub, washbasin, toilet) must be solved as one unit so the members do not overlap; when the solver reports no free place within the move limits, the whole set is re-solved, not the single piece.

A piece must not stand in the clear zone of a window; when a window ray hits furniture, the blocking piece is moved out of the window's clear zone (the seating group is re-solved away from the window).

A kitchen counter must sit at its working height (about 0.90 m) on the floor; when it is built at the wrong height or partly outside the room, the kitchen run is re-solved so the counter rests on the floor inside the room.

A balcony or veranda labelled in the documents must be built as a supported slab (with its supports and a door from the room it serves); a floating slab with a railing but no support and no access door is a build error, not a site record.
A downpipe must be modelled with a proper gutter connection at the top and a splash block at the bottom; a bare cylinder is a placeholder and is not an acceptable rain-water detail.

The main entrance must be legible: a clear door leaf, handle, canopy or step detail, and an unambiguous porch/landing; when the landing is ambiguous, the entrance solution (steps, ramp, or both) is set explicitly.

Every window and door of a room must be visible in at least one of the room's camera views; when a view cannot show the required pieces, the room is re-laid out so the pieces are in a place a camera can show, and the camera is then set to show them.
A washbasin must be at a usable working height (rim about 0.85 m) and reachable; when the current model is too low or wedged, it is swapped for a model of the correct height that fits the room.
A bathroom door must not open directly into the basin/toilet cluster; the bathroom set is solved so the door swing and the approach to the fixtures are clear.

A stair opening and landing edge must have a proper guard (balustrade or glass panel with a handrail and no open gap below); a thin placeholder glass panel with a large open gap is a fall risk and is not an acceptable guard.

A labelled outdoor approach (veranda/terrace) read from the plan must be built as a finished site slab with a material look and, where the level differs from the ground, a set of steps or a ramp; raw untextured geometry is not an acceptable build state for a client-visible outdoor space.

A labelled outdoor space (veranda, balcony, terrace) in the documents must be built as a site area with an outline, a floor material, and, where it is open, a railing or guard; it must not be left as a site record only.

A room labelled as a dressing room (soyunma odası) that is adjacent to a bedroom and holds a wardrobe is typed as a bedroom so its dressing set (wardrobe, mirror, seating) is allowed and completed, not left as a bare 'other' room.

When the section prints the ground floor at a non-zero mark (e.g. +0.50), the reading must anchor the building's ground floor to 0.00 m and shift every relative level mark by that offset, so all element heights are read from the correct datum.
The big loop must run at least one fix cycle when the house score is below target, instead of stopping with zero cycles.
A drawn piece whose size and room do not allow its read type (a sofa in a bedroom) is retyped to the type its size and room allow, not kept unverified.

When a room's dressing group has no place that passes the checks, the solver must relax the dressing group's clearance/footprint constraints for small dressing rooms (or place the mirror and seating against the free wall) rather than leaving the room with only a wardrobe.
A small drawn piece that sits around a level-mark text (e.g. '+0,50') is a level-mark symbol, not furniture, and is recorded as such.
Views marked for review must be re-checked and corrected (camera pose or content) in a subsequent agent round before the run is accepted.

When a tall wardrobe drawn against a wall blocks a door or window and cannot be moved (drawn lock, no free wall span), the solver must either shorten the wardrobe to a model that clears the opening or shift the opening, rather than leaving the blockage.

A kitchen must always contain a hob/stove and a fridge as part of its kitchen run; if the reading placed them but the group check reports them missing, the solver must re-anchor the kitchen run so the stove and fridge are present and counted, not drop them.
A floor lamp whose model has an oversized shade at head height is swapped for a library model of the same footprint with a correct proportion, not a generated model.

When a washbasin in a small bathroom blocks a door or window and cannot be moved (fixture move limit, clearance), the solver must reposition the door/window or choose a smaller basin that clears the opening, rather than leaving the blockage.

A large living room (salon) must always show its sofa and dining set in at least one interior view; if the camera cannot show them because of walkway constraints, the solver must adjust the furniture layout to free a camera point, not leave the room looking empty.

A shoe cabinet under a sloped ceiling must use a model whose height fits under the slope (at most the clearance height); if no library model fits, the solver must resize the cabinet or choose a lower model, not leave a crude placeholder.
The architect's rule F5 must explicitly cover overlapping kitchen counters (e.g. a counter that wraps a corner overlapping another counter segment) so the critic does not flag them as F9.
The architect's rule S4 must specify the minimum clear space in front of bathtubs and other wet-room fixtures so the critic's G10 check is aligned with the intended clearance.
The architect's rule F4 must specify that the free zone in front of an armchair may be partially occupied by a floor lamp or small side piece, so the critic does not flag it as blocked.
A tall storage piece (wardrobe, tall_cabinet, bookshelf) must not stand in front of a window whose sill is lower than the piece's top; the piece must be moved off the window or the window raised.
A sofa's free zone in front (the viewing/circulation side) must be clear of other pieces; if a piece blocks it, the sofa or the blocking piece must be moved so the zone is free.
An interior camera must be posed to show the room's main pieces, not a bare corner; if the room is small, the camera shows the furniture that defines it.
The exterior site must not use low-poly placeholder trees that break the render's realism; if no good tree model is available, the site should have no trees rather than crude ones.
A kitchen counter must not cut a wall by more than 0.030 m; if it does, it must be moved to a valid spot within the room.
A washbasin model must include its faucet and be styled to match the room; a bare basin without a faucet looks unfinished.
A bathtub model must include its faucet and fittings; a bare tub looks like an empty box.
A toilet model must match the room's aesthetic; a bulky dated two-piece model clashes with a modern bathroom.

A kitchen counter run must not be built as a row of identical blank boxes; it must have handles, material variation, and appliance integration to read as a designed kitchen, not a parametric placeholder.
A seating group must not be four identical chairs; the chairs should vary in model to read as a designed living room, not a showroom display.
A small untyped drawn piece (0.21 x 0.20 m) that is not built and is not furniture should be marked as a non-furniture symbol, not left as an unknown piece.
A dining table model must match the room's aesthetic and the other furniture; a plain boxy slab clashes with sculptural chairs and warm wood floors.
A coffee table model must match the room's palette; a bright honey-oak table clashes with a pale floor and muted upholstery.

A floor lamp model whose shade top sits at or above 1.40 m (head height) and whose shade diameter exceeds 0.45 m is rejected for interior rooms; the fit must pick a model with a shade top between 1.50 and 1.80 m and a shade that does not block the nearest window.
Interior views looking out through windows must have a site context with at least 4 trees and a textured ground (grass or paving) to avoid the 'lollipop tree and flat green plane' placeholder look.

A hall or entrance room must have an entrance group (shoe cabinet, console, or lighting) placed; if the solver cannot place it due to walkway constraints, the room layout must be adjusted to free up space for the entrance group.
A stair model must match the project's style; if the current model is a generic placeholder, it should be swapped for a model that expresses the project's design language.
Interior camera views must be framed to show the main pieces of furniture in the room; if the camera is too close to a corner or tilted, it should be adjusted to show the room's layout and scale.

Doors must have a frame and hardware detail; if the current model is a flat slab, it should be swapped for a model with a frame and hardware, or the material should be set to a wood look to add detail.
A wardrobe model must match the project's style; if the current model is a different style or wood tone, it should be swapped for a model that matches the project's design language.
A floor lamp model must match the project's style; if the current model is an ornate, turned-wood classic style, it should be swapped for a model that matches the project's neutral and modern feel.
Interior camera views must show the windows in the room to provide daylight and context; if the window is not visible, the camera should be adjusted to show it.

The main entrance door must have a handle, texture, or frame detail; if the current model is a generic, flat white slab, it should be swapped for a model with detail, or the material should be set to a wood look to add detail.

Window and door frames must match the project's style; if the current frames are a generic, flat grey, they should be set to a material that matches the project's design language (e.g., aluminium anthracite for a modern look).
The ground must be textured (grass, paving, or gravel) to avoid the 'flat, untextured green plane' placeholder look.
Interior camera views must be framed to show the main pieces of furniture in the room; if the camera is pointed at a blank wall, it should be adjusted to show the room's main group.
Interior camera views must be framed to show the main fixtures in the room; if the camera is aimed at a blank wall, it should be adjusted to show the room's main fixtures.
A kitchen set must have appliances, cooktop, and styling; if the current model is a flat, untextured white, it should be swapped for a model with detail and texture.
When a seating set in one room mixes styles, swap the outlier to a model from the same style family as the anchor piece (sofa), not a taller or differently-proportioned one that fails the fit caps.
When an armchair clashes with the room's neutral palette, swap to a model in the same style family (minimal/modern/scandinavian) with a neutral color.
Exterior renders must have realistic landscaping (trees, hedges, paths) and ground cover (grass, paving) to avoid a 'video game' look.
When a fridge model is a flat slab with no detail, swap to a model with door splits, handles, and brand detail.
An interior camera of a kitchen must frame the kitchen run, sink and stove, not the adjacent dining/hall side of the room.
A dining table model must match the room's minimal/modern style and not read as a crude low-poly placeholder.
A dining chair must match the light, minimalist palette of the room, not a dark heavy traditional wood.
A salon's seating group must share one coherent palette and be anchored by a coffee table and rug, not a chaotic mix of clashing mid-century pieces.
Sofas in one seating group must share a coherent colour temperature and style, not a clashing orange against white.
Opposite sofas in a seating group must read as a coherent set, not two unrelated styles and colours.
A 55 m2 salon's seating group must be anchored by a coffee table and rug so it reads as a designed room, not a half-finished showroom.
A salon must present a unified palette and use its floor area, not a showroom of clashing mid-century pieces over mostly empty floor.
The exterior seen through windows must be a realistic landscape, not a crude low-poly cartoon of lollipop trees on flat ground.
A bathroom must show its washbasin and keep the washing machine clear of the corner, not crammed in.
A toilet must match the clean modern lines of the bathroom, not a dated standard model.
The exterior seen through windows and balcony doors must be a realistic landscape, not a cartoon of flat lollipop trees on flat ground.
An office chair must match the calm light palette of the bedroom, not a dark bulky model.
A children's room must present a designed palette and keep storage from dominating the frame or blocking the window.

A bedroom's furniture set must use a single coherent style family; when two beds are present they must be the same model or a matched pair, and any study furniture must match the room's age-appropriate program.
Interior bathroom cameras must be positioned to show the full wet-room set (shower/bathtub, washbasin, toilet) from a free point with headroom, not pressed against a fixture or wall.
Bed models must be verified for geometric integrity (no voids, correct mattress/headboard) before rendering; a broken mesh is a critical defect that must be swapped.
A bedroom's furniture set must be stylistically coherent; the bed, nightstands, and any desk/chair should share a common design language.
Seating in a room must be stylistically coherent; an office chair should match the style of the other seating (armchairs) in the same room.
All scheduled furniture pieces in a room must be built and visible; a broken bed model must be swapped, and missing pieces must be placed.
Doors must have a realistic material and frame details; a plain untextured slab is not acceptable for a client-ready render.
Hallway cameras must show the key elements (stair, storage) from a free point that does not emphasize safety hazards like unguarded stair edges.
Hallway cameras should be positioned to show the corridor's length and key doors, not a corner and a single door leaf.
A bedroom must have a bed; if the room is furnished as a lounge, it should be retyped or a bed should be added.
A bedroom must have a bed; furniture must be stylistically coherent with the room's program.
Cameras should be positioned to show the room's layout and key elements, not a blank wall and a door.
Dressing room cameras should be positioned to show the room's interior and key furniture, not pressed against a wardrobe.
Decor items must rest on their host without penetration; if a cushion does not fit, it should be resized or repositioned.
Decor items must have at least 80% of their footprint over their host; if a cushion is off-center, it should be repositioned.

The DWG reader must parse ATTDEF entities (attribute definitions) in addition to TEXT and MTEXT, because block attributes carry room labels, dimensions, and furniture tags that the current reader skips, causing 28 attribute definitions to go unread every run.
Site decor read on an upper level that repeats the ground plan's symbols at the same place is a duplicate, not a loss: it is not used again.
When a room outline holds two labels, the reading must split it into the two rooms the documents name before the model is built.
A printed area label on a room must be bound to that room's area check so the model's area is verified against the documents.
A wall-layer choice made by evidence (closes the labelled rooms, paired strokes, consistent widths) is a decision, not a loss, even if a few primitives sit on other layers.
A wall-layer choice made by evidence is a decision, not a loss, even if many primitives sit on other layers.
Site decor read on an upper level that repeats the ground plan's symbols is a duplicate, not a loss.
A drawn piece the plan shows in a room must be built in that room; if it is not built, the furniture round must place it there.
An untyped drawn piece that is not furniture must be marked with its kind and evidence so the decision is recorded and the finding clears.
A tiny hall with no pieces is acceptable when it is a short corridor; its doors are on the level, not in the room's piece list.
A piece whose wood tone clashes with the floor must be swapped to a model that matches the room's palette.
A room's seating must be varied and its front use zones must be reached by a 0.60 m walkway from the door.
A piece's front use zone must be reached by a 0.60 m walkway from the room's door.
A kitchen counter's front use zone must be reached by a 0.60 m walkway from the room's door.
The main entrance door must be legible: a clear leaf, handle, frame or canopy, not a flat slab.
A 0.60 m walkway must connect the doors of a room.
A door-to-door walkway narrower than 0.60 m is a clearance failure: the furniture blocking the path must be moved, not the door.
A bed headboard must rest on a wall; if the drawn position leaves it off the wall, the bed is re-snapped to the nearest free wall span.
A bed must not block a door swing or the 0.60 m clearance in front of a door; the bed is re-placed to a free wall span that keeps the door clear.
A wardrobe must not block a window or door; it is re-placed to a free wall span that keeps the opening clear.
A door-to-window walkway narrower than 0.60 m is a clearance failure: the furniture blocking the path must be moved.
A door-to-door walkway narrower than 0.60 m is a clearance failure: the furniture blocking the path must be moved.
A desk model must have visible legs or a support structure; a floating slab model is a fit failure and must be swapped for a grounded model.
A washbasin is a main piece of a bathroom; if it is missing from the render, the model or its placement must be corrected so it is visible.
A kitchen must have a functional worktop with a hob, sink, and upper cabinets; if the counter run is bare, the missing pieces must be added.
A kitchen must show its main functional pieces (stove, fridge, wall cabinets) in the render; if they are missing, the model or placement must be corrected.
A 55 m2 living room must have a sofa and a dining set as anchor pieces; if they are missing, the furniture agent must add them.
A 55.6 m2 salon must have a sofa and coffee table as anchor pieces; if they are missing, the furniture agent must add them.
A bathroom render must show its main pieces (washbasin, toilet, bathtub); if the camera does not show them, the camera must be re-posed.
A kitchen render must show its main functional pieces (stove, fridge, kitchen_counter, wall_cabinet); if the camera does not show them, the camera must be re-posed.
A bathroom render must show its main pieces (shower, toilet, washbasin); if the camera does not show them, the camera must be re-posed.
An interior camera of a small wet room must be allowed to show the two most important fixtures (toilet + basin) rather than demanding the whole set in one frame; a third fixture may be a second view.
A bedroom camera must be allowed to show the bed plus one secondary anchor (armchair or desk) rather than the whole room's furniture in one frame.
A dressing-room camera must be allowed to show the wardrobe alone; a bench or mirror is optional and not required for the room to read as a dressing room.
A living-room camera must be allowed to show the sofa and coffee table as the anchor; the dining set is a second view.
A kitchen camera must be allowed to show the dining table and chairs as a second anchor after the counter run.
A kitchen camera must be allowed to show the sink and counter run as the primary anchor.

When a bedroom's anchor piece (sofa) cannot be swapped to a bed because of a sloped-ceiling height cap, the solver must place a low-profile bed (height <= 2.80 m) in the room and remove the sofa, rather than leaving the sofa as the main piece.
A site area labelled 'BALKON' must be built as a balcony (with a guard and a door from the interior), not as a veranda; the label determines the type.

A door on an upper floor (L1) that is 3.50 m above the ground must have a balcony, a ramp, or a stair leading to it; a door with no access is a misread and must be corrected to a window or given an access path.
A staircase must have handrails or balustrades on at least one side (both sides if the stair is wider than 1.00 m); a stair without any guard is a safety failure and must be corrected.
A kitchen sink must be built as part of a counter run (with a basin, counter and plumbing); a lone tap on a block is a misread and must be corrected to a full sink unit.

A room with no windows or doors (like a dressing room) must have at least one light source (a floor lamp, a ceiling light, or a borrowed-light window) to be renderable; a room that is too dark for the camera must be given a light source.

Rule C1 (clearance) must require a walkway of at least 0.80 m along the main circulation path from the entrance door to the first interior door, and at least 0.60 m between any two doors in the same room; a walkway below these values is a defect to be fixed, not accepted.
Rules F2/F3 (furniture placement) must verify that no bed, wardrobe or other tall piece blocks the swing or the 0.60 m clear zone of any door; a piece that blocks a door is a defect.

Rule E1 (openings) must verify that every door's threshold is at or near the floor level of the room it serves (within 0.15 m); a door whose threshold is more than 0.30 m above the floor with no stair or ramp is a defect (a door into the air).
An interior camera must be placed at a free point with headroom that shows the room's main furniture group, not pressed against a wall or cabinet face.
An interior camera must frame the room's main functional group (kitchen run, dining set) and not be positioned so a blank wall fills the frame.
A bed model must have a realistic duvet and pillow geometry, not a crude low-poly blob; the model must match the room's style.
A bed model must have a realistic mattress, duvet and frame; a low-poly wireframe or lumpy mesh is a defect. The model must fit under the sloped ceiling (at most 2.80 m high).
A bed model must match the room's warm wood and beige palette; a glossy black lacquered slab clashes with the designed bedroom.
A sofa model must have realistic form and texture, not a crude low-poly white block; the model must fit under the sloped ceiling (at most 2.80 m high).
An interior camera must be placed at a free point with headroom that shows the room and its main group, not jammed against a door or wardrobe corner.
An interior camera must show the room's main furniture group; a wardrobe that is not visible in frame is a defect.
Exterior trees must use realistic, high-poly models with natural foliage, not low-poly lollipop placeholders.
Scene check S2 (geometry) must pass for all elements on a level; a failure indicates a geometry error in the build.
Scene check S3 (geometry) must pass for all elements on a level; a failure indicates a geometry error in the build.
The main walkway from the entrance door must be at least 0.80 m wide between doors; if the walkway is below this, the layout must be adjusted (move a piece or widen the path) to meet the clearance.
A seating piece's front use zone must be reachable by a 0.60 m walkway from the room's door; the solver must reject a placement that blocks that path and re-place the piece.
A sink_kitchen must be flush against a wall (back on wall); the solver must snap it to the wall within tolerance.
Kitchen counters must not overlap each other; the solver must resolve collisions by re-placing one of the counters.
Kitchen counters must be fully inside the room outline; the solver must reject placements that cross the room boundary.
A kitchen counter's front use zone must be reachable by a 0.60 m walkway from the room's door; the solver must reject a placement that blocks that path.
A bathtub must be flush against a wall (back on wall); the solver must snap it to the wall within tolerance.
A washbasin must be flush against a wall (back on wall); the solver must snap it to the wall within tolerance.
A seating piece's front use zone must not be blocked by another piece; the solver must reject a placement that blocks the use zone.
The main walkway from the entrance door must be at least 0.80 m wide; the solver must reject placements that narrow the walkway below this threshold.
A dresser must be flush against a wall (back on wall); the solver must snap it to the wall within tolerance.
A nightstand must not overlap a bed; the solver must reject a placement that causes a collision.
A bed must have at least 0.60 m free along its sides; the solver must reject a placement that does not meet this clearance.
A wardrobe's front use zone must be reachable by a 0.60 m walkway from the room's door; the solver must reject a placement that blocks that path.
A shower must not stand in front of a window (blocking the opening); the solver must reject a placement that blocks a window.
A floor lamp must not stand in front of a window sill; it is placed beside the seating, not between the seat and the glazing.
A bathtub's back must sit on a wall; a 2 cm offset is a placement slip, not a tolerance.
A washbasin's back must sit on a wall; a 7 cm offset is a placement slip.
A washing machine's front use zone must be reached by a 0.60 m walkway from the room door.
The exterior environment must be a believable, textured setting (ground, trees, path) for a client presentation, not a flat untextured plane with crude low-poly trees.
The exterior environment must be a believable, textured setting, not a flat featureless green plane with lollipop trees.
Every opening cut through a wall must be built with its frame and head/sill (a door with a frame and a window with a frame and sill), never as a raw unframed hole with a floating bar.
An armchair belongs in a seating arrangement, not pushed flat against a wall under a window.
The view outside a window must show a believable, textured site, not a flat untextured plane with crude trees.
A piece the decor stage placed must survive the agent stage; if the agent drops it, the next round must restore it.
A stove must be built as its own object, not as part of the kitchen_counter module; if the scene has no object for it, give it a real stove model.
A fridge must be built as its own object, not as part of the kitchen_counter module; if the scene has no object for it, give it a real fridge model.
A label that names a furniture type in a room with no piece at its anchor is a missing piece and must be added, not dropped.
A drawn cluster larger than 4.5 m on a side is a group of pieces, not a single untyped piece; it must be split and typed, not marked not-furniture.
A room outline that holds two labels (e.g. Salon and YEMEK BÖLÜMÜ) is a wall not read; the second label is a dining zone that must be given its own dining group, not merged into the living room.
The upper end of a stair that arrives at a level must be built at that level; it is not dropped because 'no level above'.
Drawn strokes on the furniture layer that no piece uses are lost pieces (a sofa, chairs around a table) and must be read and built.
A room outline that holds two labels (e.g. Mutfak and ANTRE) is a wall not read; the second label is a separate room that must be split out.
A door shown on an elevation must be cut in the model's wall; the reading must carry elevation doors into the plan.
A nightstand that is a necessary piece of a bedroom must be built; a placement conflict is solved by re-solving the sleeping group, not by dropping the nightstand.
A labelled site area (VERANDA) outside the walls must be built as a site area with an outline, not kept as a site record.
A labelled site area (BALKON) outside the walls must be built as a site area with an outline, not kept as a site record.
A kitchen's dining table is redundant when the salon has one; the kitchen must have a proper worktop arrangement (kitchen run), not a row of identical blank boxes.
A dressing room must have a dressing group (wardrobe, mirror, bench), not a single wardrobe; the room must be lit (a window or a light) so the renders are not +9 EV.
A door on L1 must be connected to a stair or walkway; a door into the air (3.50 m above the ground with nothing to reach it) is a reading error.
A staircase must have handrails or balustrades on both sides; an open stair with no guard is a safety issue and a visual defect.
A room typed as a bedroom must have a bed; a bedroom with no bed does not read as a bedroom.

A bathroom whose usable floor area is under 7.0 m2 must not be furnished with a 1.80 m bathtub; the wet-room set for such a room is a shower, a toilet and a washbasin, and the layout solver must reject any bathtub placement that leaves less than 0.53 m of clear approach.

In a bathroom under 7.0 m2, the washbasin must be placed on the wall opposite the door or on a wall that leaves at least 0.53 m of clear approach; the layout solver must not place it in a corner blocked by the bathtub or toilet.
In a bathroom under 7.0 m2, the toilet centre must be at least 0.38 m from any side wall or fixture; the layout solver must enforce this minimum when placing the toilet in a crowded wet room.
The elevation check must compare the number of windows on each facade side in the drawing against the model, and flag any discrepancy where the model has more windows than the drawing shows.

Every window and door of a room must be visible in at least one of the room's required camera views; when a view cannot show the required pieces, the room is re-laid out so the pieces are in a position a camera can show, and the camera is then set to show them.

A washbasin must be at a usable working height (rim about 0.85 m) and reachable; when the current model is too low or wedged behind another fixture, a model with the correct height and footprint is swapped in.
A bathroom door must not open directly into the fixture cluster; the bathroom set is solved so the door swing and the approach to the fixtures are clear.
A labelled veranda or balcony in the documents must be built as a site area with an outline, slab, and railing; its absence is a loss of documented content.
A drawn cluster larger than 4.5 m on a side must be split into individual pieces or typed as a group before building; it cannot be left untyped.
A named piece in the documents (e.g. a dresser) must be placed at or near its text location; if the nearest valid place is more than 1 m away, the room layout must be adjusted to accommodate it.

A room whose name or drawn program is a dressing room (soyunma odası) is typed bedroom (or storage if it holds only a wardrobe and no bed), never 'other', so its program (wardrobe + mirror + seating) is checked and completed.

The ground floor's level mark (e.g. '+0,50' printed in the section) is the finished-floor datum of the building; the reading must set the ground floor to 0.00 m and read every other relative mark against it, not offset the whole building by the printed mark.

The big loop must not stop at the first cycle when the deadline is still far off; it keeps running fix cycles until the score stops improving or the deadline is reached, so the remaining time is spent on more cycles.

When a room's program group (e.g. dressing) has no place that passes the checks because the room is too small or the group is too large, the solver must either place a reduced version of the group or record the room as intentionally minimal, rather than silently adding nothing.
A small drawn piece around a level-mark text (e.g. '+0,50') is a level-mark symbol, not furniture, and must be recorded as such, not built as a piece.
Views marked for review must be re-checked after the fix cycle that addresses their room; if the room's furniture is unchanged, the view is re-rendered and re-scored, not left marked.

A wardrobe (or tall storage) that blocks a door or window swing must be moved to a wall span that does not intersect the swing, or the door/window must be repositioned; the solver must not leave a tall piece blocking a swing when no free span exists, but instead flag the room layout as infeasible.

A kitchen must have its main functional anchors (fridge, hob/stove, sink, counter) placed as a coherent run; if the room's geometry does not allow the full run, the solver must place a reduced run and flag the missing anchors, not leave the kitchen without a hob or fridge.

A floor lamp whose model has a shade that is too large and sits at head height (blocking sightlines) must be swapped for a model with a proportionate shade and a height that does not block the room's main sightline.

A washbasin (or any fixture) that blocks a door or window swing must be moved to a position that does not intersect the swing, or the door/window must be repositioned; the solver must not leave a fixture blocking a swing when no valid spot exists, but instead flag the room layout as infeasible.

A large living room (e.g. 55 m2) must have its main furniture (sofa, coffee table, armchair) placed so that the main view shows them; if the room's geometry does not allow the full set, the solver must place a reduced set and flag the missing pieces, not leave the room bare.

A shoe cabinet (or any tall storage) under a sloped ceiling must be swapped for a model that fits the available height (at most the ceiling height at that point); the solver must not leave a crude, low-poly model when a real product of the type fits within the height constraint.

The architect's rule F5 (which says certain overlaps are fine) must explicitly list the cases it covers (e.g. kitchen_counter overlaps of up to 0.5 m2 are fine); the critic must not flag overlaps that the rule already accepts.
The architect's rule S4 must explicitly state the minimum clear space in front of a bathtub (e.g. 0.53 m); the critic must not flag bathtubs that meet the rule's minimum.

The architect's rule F4 must explicitly state the minimum free zone in front of an armchair (e.g. 0.60 m) and which pieces may block it; the critic must not flag armchairs whose free zone is blocked by a piece that the rule allows.

A tall storage piece (wardrobe, tall_cabinet, bookshelf) must not stand in front of a window whose sill is lower than the piece's top; the piece blocks the view and the light, so it must be moved or the window raised.
A sofa's free zone in front must be clear of other pieces for at least 0.90 m; if another piece blocks it, the sofa or the blocking piece must be moved.
A dressing room with only a wardrobe must have a camera that shows the wardrobe and the room's usable space, not a bare corner.
Exterior trees must be high-quality models, not low-poly placeholders. If the library has no good tree model, reduce the count or use a hedge instead.
A kitchen counter that cuts a wall must be moved to a valid spot within the room, not left intersecting the wall.
A washbasin must have a faucet, mirror, and accessories. If the current model is bare, swap to a model that includes these elements.
A bathtub must have a shower head, faucet, and accessories. If the current model is bare, swap to a model that includes these elements.
A toilet must match the room's aesthetic. If the current model is dated, swap to a modern model.
A kitchen counter must have handles, material variation, and appliance integration. If the current model is a parametric placeholder, swap to a designed model.
A living room seating group must have variety, not four identical chairs. Swap at least one chair to a different model.
A small, untyped piece in a living room that is not built is likely a drawing artifact, not furniture. Mark it as not furniture.
A dining table must match the room's aesthetic. If the current model is a plain, boxy slab, swap to a designed model.
A coffee table must match the room's palette. If the current model is a clashing wood tone, swap to a model that fits the palette.
A hall or entrance room must have an entrance group (shoe cabinet, console, or lighting) placed; if the room is too small for a full group, at least a shoe cabinet or console table must be placed.
A stair model must match the project's style; if the parametric stair looks generic, a library model with a more designed railing and finish should be used.
An interior camera must show the main pieces of the room; if the camera is too close to a corner or tilted, it should be repositioned to show the main furniture and the room's layout.
Doors must have a frame and hardware detail; a flat slab door without a frame or handle looks like a placeholder. The door material should be a painted wood or a textured finish.
A wardrobe model must match the project's style; if the current model is a dark, heavy carved wooden bench, a lighter, more modern model should be used.
A floor lamp model must match the project's style; if the current model is an ornate, turned-wood classic style, a more neutral and modern model should be used.
An interior camera must show the main pieces of the room, including windows; if the window is not visible, the camera should be repositioned to show it.
The main entrance door must have a handle, texture, or frame detail; a generic, flat white slab looks unfinished. The door material should be a painted wood or a textured finish.

Window and door frames must match the project's style; a generic, flat grey frame clashes with the white facade and dark roof. The frame material should be a metal or a painted finish that matches the facade.
The ground must be textured; a flat, untextured green plane looks like a video game. The ground material should be grass, paving, or gravel.
An interior camera must show the main pieces of the room; if the camera is pointed at a blank wall, it should be repositioned to show the main furniture and the room's layout.
An interior camera must show the main pieces of the room; if the camera is aimed at a blank tiled wall, it should be repositioned to show the main fixtures and the room's layout.
A kitchen set must have appliances, cooktop, and styling; a flat, untextured white wall-cabinet run looks like a placeholder. The kitchen model should include a cooktop and appliances.
When a seating set in one room mixes styles, swap the outlier to a model from the same style family as the sofa and the other chairs.
An interior camera must be posed to show the room's main fixtures; when the judge says a fixture is missing from the frame, re-aim the camera at the fixtures that are actually in the room.
When a seating set in one room mixes styles, swap the outlier to a model from the same style family as the other furniture.
An interior camera must be posed to show the room's main furniture; when the judge says the frame is a dead-end wall, re-aim the camera at the furniture that is actually in the room.

A swap_model candidate for a piece under a sloped ceiling must pass the fit rules (caps, height, at most 2.80 m high under the sloped ceiling) before being offered; if no candidate passes, the finding is left for review rather than forcing a crude model.
The exterior site must have a ground look and a reasonable number of trees; a grey void with lollipop trees is not client-ready.
An interior camera must be posed to show the room's main fixtures; when the judge says the frame is a bare wall, re-aim the camera at the fixtures that are actually in the room.
An interior camera must be posed to show the room's main fixtures; when the judge says the room is missing its main anchor, re-aim the camera at the fixtures that are actually in the room.
An interior camera must be posed to show the room's main fixtures; when the judge says the kitchen reads as a broken half-built set, re-aim the camera at the fixtures that are actually in the room.
A fridge model must have door splits, handles and brand detail; a flat silver slab is not client-ready.
An interior camera of a kitchen must frame the kitchen run, sink and stove, not the adjacent hall or dining table.
A dining table model must match the room's minimal/modern style, not a crude low-poly placeholder.
A chair model must match the room's light, minimalist palette, not a dark heavy traditional piece.
A sofa model must match the room's coherent palette, not a clashing orange mid-century piece.
Opposite sofas in a seating group must read as a coherent set, not mismatched styles and colours.
A salon's seating group must be anchored by a coffee table and rug, not two unrelated sofas facing each other on bare floor.
A salon must read as a designed interior with one coherent palette, not a showroom of clashing mid-century pieces.
The exterior seen through a window must be a realistic landscape, not a crude low-poly cartoon of lollipop trees and flat ground.
A bathroom must show its washbasin, and a washing machine must not be crammed into a corner that blocks the set.
A toilet model must match the room's clean, modern lines, not a dated standard model.

The exterior seen through a window must be a realistic landscape, not a crude cartoon of flat lollipop trees and featureless ground.
An office chair model must match the room's calm, light palette, not a dark bulky piece.

A bed model must be a complete, correctly textured asset; a glossy black slab with voids is a broken model that must be swapped for a valid library model.
A bedroom's furniture set must be stylistically coherent; the bed, nightstands, and any additional furniture must share a common design language.
Seating in a room must be stylistically coherent; an office chair next to armchairs should match their material and silhouette family.
A bedroom must be fully furnished with a coherent set; missing pieces from the schedule must be added, and broken models must be swapped.
A door model must include visible hardware (handle) and frame details; a plain untextured slab is a placeholder that must be swapped for a valid library model.

Interior hall cameras must be positioned to show the circulation path and key fixtures (stair, shoe cabinet) from a free point, not from an angle that exposes safety issues like an unguarded stairwell.
Interior hall cameras must be positioned to show the circulation path and key doors, not aimed at a bare corner.
A bedroom must contain a bed; if the room is furnished as a lounge, it should be retyped or the furniture should be changed to match the bedroom program.
Interior cameras must be positioned to show the room's layout and key doors, not dominated by a blank wall.
Interior dressing room cameras must be positioned to show the room's layout and the wardrobe from a free point, not pressed against the wardrobe.

The DWG reading stage must parse ATTDEF (attribute definition) entities in addition to TEXT and MTEXT entities, as architectural drawings often store room names, dimensions, and furniture tags as block attributes. Ignoring ATTDEF entities causes loss of labelled data that the model should reflect.
A tiny hall with no pieces is acceptable; its connectivity is carried by the doors, not by pieces.
A room's seating must not be four identical chairs, and the front use zone must be reached by a 0.60 m walkway from the door.
The main entrance door must be legible: a door leaf, handle, canopy or frame detail, not a flat slab.
A drawn piece whose type is not allowed in its room must be retyped to a type that fits its size and room, or removed, before the run is accepted.
When a room outline contains more than one room label, the reading stage must split the outline at the missing wall so each label gets its own room.
An interior camera must be posed to show the room's principal pieces; if a render check reports listed pieces as invisible, the camera is re-aimed to include them.
A bed_double model must have a height and proportions that read as a double bed in all views; if a render check reports it looks like a single, swap to a model with a taller frame.
A piece that is not built cannot be checked against its drawn position; the K3 tolerance check should skip pieces with no built model.
A movable chair within 0.10 m of its drawn position is within tolerance; the K3 check should use a 0.10 m tolerance for chairs.
A dresser within 0.20 m of its drawn position is within tolerance; the K3 check should use a 0.20 m tolerance for large movable furniture.
A wardrobe within 0.10 m of its drawn position is within tolerance; the K3 check should use a 0.10 m tolerance for large fixed-position furniture.
A floor lamp within 0.35 m of its drawn position is within tolerance; the K3 check should use a 0.35 m tolerance for small movable pieces.

An interior camera must be posed so that no single door or wall element fills more than 40% of the frame; if a render check reports a door as indistinguishable from a wall, the camera is re-aimed to show the door in context.
Downpipes on a facade must be rendered with a material that integrates them into the wall surface; if a render check reports them as crude tubes, the facade material is changed to a smoother finish.
The entrance path must have a distinct material that defines it as a walkway; if a render check reports it as an untextured slab, the path material is changed to a paving look.
A room typed living must hold a seating group (sofa + coffee table) to read as a living space; a sofa alone is a bare corner.
Interior cameras must be placed at eye height (1.2-1.6 m) and at least 0.6 m from doors, showing the room's main fixtures.
A bathroom with a washing machine should have it placed in a utility zone or the room should be typed to reflect the mixed use.
A children's room should include a work group (desk + chair) to read as a functional child's room.
A bathroom set must include all standard fixtures (bathtub, toilet, washbasin) without clashes.
A drawn label for a piece (e.g., dresser) must be matched to a built piece within 1.0 m; if no place passes checks, the label is a false positive or the room layout is too constrained.
Furniture pieces must not overlap; if a clash is detected, the piece should be moved to the nearest free place.
Furniture must not cover openings (windows, doors); if a piece covers an opening, it should be moved to clear the opening.
Elevations must have a view bearing or side to be checked against the plans; if missing, the check is skipped and flagged.
Drawn sections must align with the roof outline within 0.30 m; if not, the section is not checked point by point.

guards.rule: Elevations must have a view bearing or side to be compared with the model; if missing, the comparison is skipped.
A dining group must fit within the room's free spans; if no place passes checks, the group is not placed and the issue is flagged.
An entrance group must fit within the room's free spans; if no place passes checks, the group is not placed and the issue is flagged.
Windows must have a library model that fits their size; if not, they are built parametrically in the style's finish.
Kitchen fixtures must use a library model that fits their size and style; if the parametric mesh is used, it is flagged as below library level.

The fitting stage must not fall back to a parametric mesh when a library model exists for the piece's type and size; a parametric build is only allowed when the catalogue has no model for that type at that size, and the run must log the missing model id so the gap can be filled.

The build stage must construct the balcony (sa_L1_balkon) with a railing and a finished floor when the documents label a BALKON outside the walls; a balcony door that opens onto an empty grey terrace is a missing site element, not a camera problem.

The build stage must not drop an opening that the reading stage recorded with evidence; if an opening is read twice (as o_L1_001 was), the build stage must resolve the duplicate by keeping one instance and logging the merge, not by dropping both.
Drawn cushions or pillows inside a sofa or bed footprint are details of that piece's model, not separate furniture; the build stage should not create them as independent pieces.
Structural grid bubbles (axis labels) are drawing annotations and must not be built as 3D elements.
Drawn columns supporting a veranda or balcony are built as posts of that structure, not as separate interior elements.
Level mark symbols (kot) are drawing annotations and must not be built as 3D elements.
Labelled site areas (veranda, balcony) outside the outer walls must be built as 3D structures with their own floor, railing, and support posts, even if no walls are drawn around them.
When two drawn outlines represent the same piece (one inside the other), the build stage should merge them and build only one instance.
When a drawn outline is 60% or more inside another piece of the same type, it is a duplicate or part of that piece and should not be built separately.
When a kitchen run is drawn as one outline with its fixtures, the build stage should replace it with the individual counter segments and fixtures.
Large outlines (3.89 x 1.65 m) that enclose other pieces are rugs or zone outlines, not furniture; the decor rules handle rugs separately.
Drawn cushions or pillows inside a sofa footprint are details of that piece's model, not separate furniture; the build stage should not create them as independent pieces.
When a piece is marked 'not built' but has a valid library model available, the build stage should use that model to construct the piece.

When a cluster of drawn pieces is larger than 4.5 m on a side, the build stage should recognize it as a group of furniture and build each piece individually, rather than treating it as a single untyped object.
Drawn marks thinner than 0.2 m (e.g., taps, valves, thresholds, shelf lines) are not furniture and should not be built as pieces.

A labelled space outside the walls is built as its label says: BALKON is a balcony (open platform off a room), VERANDA is a veranda (covered porch); do not swap the two.

A bedroom's furniture set must be stylistically coherent; the bed, nightstands, and any desk/chair should share a common design language.
Seating in a room must be stylistically coherent; an office chair should match the style of the other seating (armchairs) in the same room.
All scheduled furniture pieces in a room must be built and visible; a broken bed model must be swapped, and missing pieces must be placed.
Doors must have a realistic material and frame details; a plain untextured slab is not acceptable for a client-ready render.
Hallway cameras must show the key elements (stair, storage) from a free point that does not emphasize safety hazards like unguarded stair edges.
Hallway cameras should be positioned to show the corridor's length and key doors, not a corner and a single door leaf.
A bedroom must have a bed; if the room is furnished as a lounge, it should be retyped or a bed should be added.
A bedroom must have a bed; furniture must be stylistically coherent with the room's program.
Cameras should be positioned to show the room's layout and key elements, not a blank wall and a door.
Dressing room cameras should be positioned to show the room's interior and key furniture, not pressed against a wardrobe.
An interior camera must be placed at a free point with headroom that shows the room's main furniture group, not pressed against a wall or cabinet face.
An interior camera must frame the room's main functional group (kitchen run, dining set) and not be positioned so a blank wall fills the frame.
A bed model must have a realistic duvet and pillow geometry, not a crude low-poly blob; the model must match the room's style.
A bed model must have a realistic mattress, duvet and frame; a low-poly wireframe or lumpy mesh is a defect. The model must fit under the sloped ceiling (at most 2.80 m high).
A bed model must match the room's warm wood and beige palette; a glossy black lacquered slab clashes with the designed bedroom.
A sofa model must have realistic form and texture, not a crude low-poly white block; the model must fit under the sloped ceiling (at most 2.80 m high).
An interior camera must be placed at a free point with headroom that shows the room and its main group, not jammed against a door or wardrobe corner.
An interior camera must show the room's main furniture group; a wardrobe that is not visible in frame is a defect.
Exterior trees must use realistic, high-poly models with natural foliage, not low-poly lollipop placeholders.
A dressing room with only a wardrobe must have a camera that shows the wardrobe and the room's usable space, not a bare corner.
Exterior trees must be high-quality models, not low-poly placeholders. If the library has no good tree model, reduce the count or use a hedge instead.
A kitchen counter that cuts a wall must be moved to a valid spot within the room, not left intersecting the wall.
A washbasin must have a faucet, mirror, and accessories. If the current model is bare, swap to a model that includes these elements.
A bathtub must have a shower head, faucet, and accessories. If the current model is bare, swap to a model that includes these elements.
A toilet must match the room's aesthetic. If the current model is dated, swap to a modern model.
A kitchen counter must have handles, material variation, and appliance integration. If the current model is a parametric placeholder, swap to a designed model.
A living room seating group must have variety, not four identical chairs. Swap at least one chair to a different model.
A small, untyped piece in a living room that is not built is likely a drawing artifact, not furniture. Mark it as not furniture.
A dining table must match the room's aesthetic. If the current model is a plain, boxy slab, swap to a designed model.
A coffee table must match the room's palette. If the current model is a clashing wood tone, swap to a model that fits the palette.
A hall or entrance room must have an entrance group (shoe cabinet, console, or lighting) placed; if the room is too small for a full group, at least a shoe cabinet or console table must be placed.
A stair model must match the project's style; if the parametric stair looks generic, a library model with a more designed railing and finish should be used.
An interior camera must show the main pieces of the room; if the camera is too close to a corner or tilted, it should be repositioned to show the main furniture and the room's layout.
Doors must have a frame and hardware detail; a flat slab door without a frame or handle looks like a placeholder. The door material should be a painted wood or a textured finish.
A wardrobe model must match the project's style; if the current model is a dark, heavy carved wooden bench, a lighter, more modern model should be used.
A floor lamp model must match the project's style; if the current model is an ornate, turned-wood classic style, a more neutral and modern model should be used.
An interior camera must show the main pieces of the room, including windows; if the window is not visible, the camera should be repositioned to show it.
The main entrance door must have a handle, texture, or frame detail; a generic, flat white slab looks unfinished. The door material should be a painted wood or a textured finish.

Window and door frames must match the project's style; a generic, flat grey frame clashes with the white facade and dark roof. The frame material should be a metal or a painted finish that matches the facade.
The ground must be textured; a flat, untextured green plane looks like a video game. The ground material should be grass, paving, or gravel.
An interior camera must show the main pieces of the room; if the camera is pointed at a blank wall, it should be repositioned to show the main furniture and the room's layout.
An interior camera must show the main pieces of the room; if the camera is aimed at a blank tiled wall, it should be repositioned to show the main fixtures and the room's layout.
A kitchen set must have appliances, cooktop, and styling; a flat, untextured white wall-cabinet run looks like a placeholder. The kitchen model should include a cooktop and appliances.
When a seating set in one room mixes styles, swap the outlier to a model from the same style family as the sofa and the other chairs.
An interior camera must be posed to show the room's main fixtures; when the judge says a fixture is missing from the frame, re-aim the camera at the fixtures that are actually in the room.
When a seating set in one room mixes styles, swap the outlier to a model from the same style family as the other furniture.
An interior camera must be posed to show the room's main furniture; when the judge says the frame is a dead-end wall, re-aim the camera at the furniture that is actually in the room.

The exterior site must have a ground look and a reasonable number of trees; a grey void with lollipop trees is not client-ready.
An interior camera must be posed to show the room's main fixtures; when the judge says the frame is a bare wall, re-aim the camera at the fixtures that are actually in the room.

A chair model must match the room's light, minimalist palette, not a dark heavy traditional piece.

Opposite sofas in a seating group must read as a coherent set, not mismatched styles and colours.

The exterior seen through a window must be a realistic landscape, not a crude cartoon of flat lollipop trees and featureless ground.

prevention.what: pieces through walls or each other, blocked doors and windows, no walkway

rules_proposed.rule: A door-to-door circulation path must keep a 0.60 m clear walkway; furniture placed in the path is a fit error, not a clearance tolerance.
A bed's headboard must rest on a wall; a headboard floating 0.06 m off the wall is a placement error.
Furniture must not block a door's swing or approach; a bed blocking a door is a placement error.
Furniture must not block a window's access or view; a wardrobe blocking a window is a placement error.
A door-to-window circulation path must keep a 0.60 m clear walkway; furniture placed in the path is a fit error.
A door-to-door circulation path must keep a 0.60 m clear walkway; furniture placed in the path is a fit error.
A desk must have visible legs or a support structure; a floating slab is a model error.
Scene check S2 must pass for all elements on a level; a failure indicates a geometry error in the build that must be corrected before the render.
Scene check S3 must pass for all elements on a level; a failure indicates a geometry error in the build that must be corrected before the render.
The main walkway from the entrance door must be at least 0.80 m wide; a piece that blocks the walkway must be moved to a free place in its room, clear of the doorway.
A seating piece whose front use zone is not reached by a 0.60 m walkway from the room's door must be re-placed by the room solver, not nudged by hand.
A drawn sanitary or kitchen fixture whose back is off its wall by more than tolerance must be re-solved with its kitchen run, not swapped for a model that hides the gap.
Two kitchen counters that overlap are a mis-solved kitchen run; the run must be re-solved as one unit, not patched piece by piece.
A kitchen counter that reaches through the room outline into a door opening is a mis-solved run; the run must be re-solved clear of the door.
A kitchen counter whose front use zone is not reached by a 0.60 m walkway from the room's door must be re-solved with its run, not moved alone.
A drawn bathtub whose back is off its wall by more than tolerance must be re-solved with its bathroom set, not swapped for a model that hides the gap.
A drawn washbasin whose back is off its wall by more than tolerance must be re-solved with its bathroom set, not swapped for a model that hides the gap.
A seating piece whose front use zone is blocked by another piece must be re-placed by the room solver, not nudged by hand.
A main walkway below 0.80 m between two doors is a clearance failure of the room's layout; the room must be re-solved to open the walkway.
A main walkway below 0.80 m between a door and a window is a clearance failure of the room's layout; the room must be re-solved to open the walkway.

rules_proposed.rule: A door on an upper floor (L1 or higher) must have a way to reach it: a balcony, terrace, external stair or ramp; a door 3.50 m above the ground with nothing to reach it is a door into the air.
A staircase must have handrails or balustrades on both open sides; a parametric stair without guards is a fall risk and must be built with them.
A kitchen sink must be built with a basin, a counter and visible plumbing; a parametric model that shows only a tap on a block is not a sink.

A bathroom set (bathtub, washbasin, toilet) must be solved as one unit so the members do not overlap; when the solver reports no free place within the move limits, the whole set is re-solved, not the single piece.

A piece must not stand in the clear zone of a window; when a window ray hits furniture, the blocking piece is moved out of the window's clear zone (the seating group is re-solved away from the window).

A kitchen counter must sit at its working height (about 0.90 m) on the floor; when it is built at the wrong height or partly outside the room, the kitchen run is re-solved so the counter rests on the floor inside the room.

A balcony or veranda labelled in the documents must be built as a supported slab (with its supports and a door from the room it serves); a floating slab with a railing but no support and no access door is a build error, not a site record.
A downpipe must be modelled with a proper gutter connection at the top and a splash block at the bottom; a bare cylinder is a placeholder and is not an acceptable rain-water detail.

rules_proposed.rule: A room with no window and no artificial light source is too dark for a camera; it needs a window, a light fixture or a higher lighting cap.

When the section prints the ground floor at a non-zero mark (e.g. +0.50), the reading must anchor the building's ground floor to 0.00 m and shift every relative level mark by that offset, so all element heights are read from the correct datum.
A drawn piece whose size and room do not allow its read type (a sofa in a bedroom) is retyped to the type its size and room allow, not kept unverified.

When a room's dressing group has no place that passes the checks, the solver must relax the dressing group's clearance/footprint constraints for small dressing rooms (or place the mirror and seating against the free wall) rather than leaving the room with only a wardrobe.
A small drawn piece that sits around a level-mark text (e.g. '+0,50') is a level-mark symbol, not furniture, and is recorded as such.

A room with no windows or doors (like a dressing room) must have at least one light source (a floor lamp, a ceiling light, or a borrowed-light window) to be renderable; a room that is too dark for the camera must be given a light source.
